The modern version of a classic bait and switch. The beta was legitimately the best part of this game because, at the time, I assumed the full release would be more fleshed out.

Boy was I wrong.

Battlefield 6 is a game that keeps showing you it could have been a real Battlefield, then immediately reminds you it chose to be something else. The gunplay is ok enough to hook you for a few matches, and there are moments where the action feels like classic Battlefield. Those moments are so rare they feel almost accidental.

A lot of it comes down to flow. Good Battlefield maps give you options. You can push the objective straight on, flank, take a side route, go up a neighboring building, or use vehicles to create pressure somewhere else. In BF6, you get funneled into the same two or three choke points, and once one team gets control, you might as well wait for the next objective. As a side note, I’m not sure who decided which maps get what vehicles and when, but that person should at least be given a stern talking to.

Maps are trash.

First off, they are tiny. The playable area alone limits options. Most maps only have a handful of lanes or are extremely flat and open. City maps are filled with locked doors and hallways that lead nowhere. Objective locations for game modes were not planned out well, and in combination with small maps and limited lanes, some rounds are not even worth playing.

For comparison:

BF6 launch maps average: 0.189 km² (9 maps)
BF4 launch maps average: 0.784 km² (8 maps I could find sizes for)
So BF4’s launch maps are about 4.15x larger.

TTK is trash too. It plays like COD so they could appeal to a larger player base.

For comparison:

In Battlefield 4, most assault rifles used the standard 24.5 max damage model, which means 5 point blank body shots to kill a 100 HP player.

So the math looks like this (stock, point blank, body shots):

AEK 971 (900 RPM, 5 shots to kill)
TTK = (shots to kill − 1) × (60 ÷ RPM)
TTK = (5 − 1) × (60 ÷ 900) = 4 × 0.0667 = 0.267s (267ms)

M416 (750 RPM, 5 shots to kill)
TTK = (5 − 1) × (60 ÷ 750) = 4 × 0.0800 = 0.320s (320ms)

ACE 23 (770 RPM, 5 shots to kill)
TTK = (5 − 1) × (60 ÷ 770) = 4 × 0.0779 = 0.312s (312ms)

Now compare that to Battlefield 6. DougS2K’s BF6 Weapon Stats Spreadsheet (posted on the Battlefield 6 subreddit and hosted on Google Sheets) has point blank body TTKs like:

TR 7: 0.167s (167ms)
M4A1: 0.200s (200ms)
B36A4: 0.250s (250ms)
M433: 0.217s (217ms)

So in BF4, typical AR gunfights are around the 312 to 320ms zone. In BF6, it can be as low as 167ms. It may not seem like much, but in game it is extremely noticeable, especially if you are a veteran Battlefield player.

Weapons…

Not even sure where to start here. I will just say that the weapons seem to contradict how the intended class playstyle is supposed to go down. The whole point of classes is tradeoffs. You pick a role, you bring certain strengths, you accept certain weaknesses, and your team makes up the difference. That is the Battlefield multiplayer identity. BF6 does not respect that. Everyone can build into everything, so class identity gets watered down into basically nothing.

Some more comparisons:

BF4: 80+ launch weapons
BF6: 45 unlockable weapons
BF6 (extra): +12 weapons via assignments after Career Rank 50

How long to unlock each weapon (worst case, last rank gated unlock):

BF4: Rank 60 total = 3,520,000 XP
25,000 XP/hr: 3,520,000 / 25,000 = 141 hrs
40,000 XP/hr: 3,520,000 / 40,000 = 88 hrs
60,000 XP/hr: 3,520,000 / 60,000 = 59 hrs

BF6: Career Rank 2 to 50 unlock track
About 72 hrs to hit Rank 50 and unlock all Career weapons (not counting the extra 12)

How long to unlock all attachments per weapon?

BF4 (kills based): 400 to 500 kills to “finish” a gun
40 KPH: 400 to 500 / 40 = 10.0 to 12.5 hrs
60 KPH: 400 to 500 / 60 = 6.7 to 8.3 hrs
90 KPH: 400 to 500 / 90 = 4.4 to 5.6 hrs

BF6 (mastery): Mastery 50, about 1,800 kills per gun
40 KPH: 1,800 / 40 = 45 hrs
60 KPH: 1,800 / 60 = 30 hrs
90 KPH: 1,800 / 90 = 20 hrs

Finally, Vehicles…

They can be fun for a bit, but nothing like previous installments. Map size and cover really limit options. Variety is also extremely limited.

For comparison:
BF4: ~50 vehicles at launch
BF6: 15 vehicles

Makes sense considering the size constraints the BF6 maps introduce. Vehicles seem like they may have been an afterthought, with no map specifically built around vehicle use.

Unfortunately, this is probably as close to classic Battlefield as EA is going to give us these days. Buy it if you want to scratch the BF itch. It will not be satisfying, but it is all you are going to get.

Once again, despite having a clear blueprint for making one of the best FPS franchises in gaming, the developers have delivered a half-baked, uninspired product. The game feels stagnant, underdeveloped, and eerily reminiscent of Battlefield 2042. In trying to appeal to everyone, it ends up appealing to no one.

The identity crisis is obvious. The game attempts to cater to Call of Duty–style players with faster movement and pacing, yet CoD players don’t want Battlefield—they already have CoD, and they quickly go back to it. Meanwhile, long-time Battlefield fans are alienated from the start. The slower, immersive experience of BF3, BF4, and BF1—defined by weighty gunplay, powerful sound design, large-scale immersion, and meaningful destruction—is largely gone.

Instead of doubling down on what made Battlefield unique, the developers once again chose microtransactions and flashy skins that feel completely out of place. These cosmetics add nothing to the experience and only further erode the franchise’s identity. What truly set Battlefield apart from its competitors—Levolution—has been stripped down to the bare minimum. Watching a crane fall is dull compared to entire buildings collapsing in BF4. Minor environmental damage doesn’t come close to the widespread, dynamic destruction seen throughout BF1, or the unforgettable cinematic moments like the zeppelin crashing mid-match.

Map design only amplifies the problem. Air vehicles are placed into maps so small and restrictive that a single dogfight can push you out of bounds nine times out of ten. The scale feels wrong, the flow feels broken, and the chaos that once defined Battlefield is missing.

From the moment the game reused the BF2042 engine, expectations were already low. While it may be an improvement over that disastrous release, it still falls far short of earning the Battlefield name. At best, it’s a slightly more polished version of a failed direction—proof that the franchise still hasn’t learned from its mistakes.

Battlefield 6 is not a Battlefield game for Battlefield veterans.

That, at its core, is fine. If Battlefield Studios want to cater to a different market, there is no problem with that.

That said, as a long time franchise veteran, with thousands of hours across Bad Company 2, BF3, BF4, BF1, and BFV... I'm just tired, man. There are other reviews with walls of gripe about this game and those of them that mention previous experience with the franchise will all say the same thing: "this game isn't for us any more." The most glaring evidence of this is the removal of class-locked weapons, and even class-locked playlists. Gone, in pursuit of something very, very different.

The maps are too crowded, too small, or too directionless. Remade maps have been shrunk, or changed to fit one particular playstyle; run and gun. A particular gripe of mine is how redundant snipers feel now. Never mind that every single sniper that has been added to the game is worse than the starting one, never mind that there is an attachment that literally zeroes the scope for you, removing half of the fun of figuring out hold points, never mind that an M4 with a couple of attachments will burst you down over 500+m quicker than you can rechamber a round if you miss your headshot... nobody even bothers. I see no snipers in this game, and when I do, they're running a rangefinder. It's boring.

The remakes of Golmud and Firestorm? Boring. The small town at the top of Golmud, which was once a main thoroughfare that could be reliably held by a few well-placed engineers? Now a sprawling close-quarters arena, with too many angles to make defence a reliable option. Just let it get taken and attack again. All of the verticality, rocks that snipers could sit on? Flattened. There's one now, at the back of the map, obstructed by the same town with no view onto other objectives. Firestorm has been shrunk, and the petroleum containers on the right side of the map which once provided a little verticality are now destructible - all but guaranteeing that if you kill someone from there, they'll just get in a tank and blow it up so you can't use it.

This game makes me physically tired to play. I'm not young. I don't particularly want to engage with the fast-paced, "sprint around like a headless chicken" form of play that this game all but incentivises. I never did in previous games, why would I want to now? Why are you giving me no other viable option?

Look, if you like fast-paced close-quarters gameplay, then I'm sure this game is perfect for you, and I would encourage you to play it, to enjoy it. But for me, and so many others, who never sought that experience in Battlefield and knew that our playstyle was just as viable in all other entries to the franchise, even 2042 for goodness sakes... it's just not there, and it's clear that Battlefield Studios only intend to move further and further away from what this franchise used to be.

What a disappointment. What a tremendous, saddening disappointment.

It really is a shame what was once my favourite game series has turned into. In the beta and at launch Battlefield 6 actually seemed decent and I was optimistic they may have finally figured out how to make a good Battlefield again and while there are improvements over 2042 it is sadly still not enough. I was expecting to put 1000+ hours into this game as I have with most other Battlefields but after just nearly 300 hours I had to admit myself it just isn't fun at all. 

The netcode wasn't great at the start but somehow it has just gotten worse as time goes on. You can immediately tell if the netcode is ''on your side'' after your first gunfight in a match and sadly it is nearly always against you. Not that having it on your side really makes it any better as you can still clearly feel the unfairness. You can accept dying in what feels like one hit and having 0 time to react or dying when you are meters behind cover already if it just happens every now and then but it is nearly every game and has only become more unbearable since launch. One of the most important things in an online fps such as this is that it at least feels fair but this game just doesn't.

The matchmaking is completely broken. Although they have never confirmed it my friends and I strongly suspect there is some sort of skill based matchmaking being used and I do believe this is why they refuse to add a server browser for official servers. Really what is the reason to not have a server browser other than if you want to force players into your matchmaking system? This again ties into the game just feeling unfair. I'm not the best player in the world but i'm no means the worst and have no problems getting into the top 5 of the scoreboard in a match but any sort of skill doesn't seem to matter when 95% of your matches are completely stacked against you. Sure you get the odd match where you're on the team that completely steamrolls the other but again there is no fun in that at all. The worst part is the extremely rare times you do get a match that is somewhat balanced and the netcode is okay the game is actually fun to play but this makes it all the more frustrating. There is a good game underneath all that but their stubbornness and inability to fix things means you rarely get to experience that. 

The content updates are also extremely disappointing. While I understand Battlefield is now a live service game 2 maps a season (that don't even release together) with 2 or 3 new guns is simply not enough and when they do things like release the little bird in season 2 it is blatantly obvious they are just holding things back to pad out seasons rather than making extra actual content. The battlepass is mostly filler too, what the game lacks in new maps and weapons there is no shortage of cosmetics and ''limited time modes'' which I guess is great if you're into that but most people aren't. I don't know a single person who would rather have another limited time mode that will be forgotten in a week over another map. The game already has the main Battlefield modes people buy it for with conquest, breakthrough, rush and a few smaller modes like TDM. Why do they insist on adding these things no one asks for? 

Portal seemed like it could be good until they yet again completely nerfed it immediately after launch. Personally i'm not someone who enjoys leaving my PC on in a portal server for hours to unlock everything but at the same time I really don't care if other people do. The game has 5000 ranks and while it doesn't seem fun if people want to just unlock all their weapons without actually engaging in pvp who cares? But the real downside to nerfing the xp in portal isn't that people can't boost its that it just automatically guarantees no one will use it. There has been some very interesting modes and maps people have created in portal that are completely dead because the simple fact is people still want to earn xp for playing and you can't do that if your server has any bots in it. They have also outright removed player created maps from other games (i.e shipment from call of duty). They provided a decent map editor that will just go to waste now. Why not have a monthly community vote or something on player created maps and add them into some sort of rotation or even turn them into actual maps? I saw several maps created from the California update alone that are all now completely dead. People are literally doing your job for you creating new maps and experiences but again they just seem to refuse to capitalise on any of it and it is so frustrating. 

I could go on but I think that gives you a good idea of where Battlefield is now. It used to be an amazing series that would take up nearly all of my time but the thought of playing it anymore is just tiring. The game will continue to haemorrhage players if they continue in this direction and sadly I don't see it changing. Look how many people have gone back to older Battlefield titles these past few days since they went on sale, you have the formula right there on how to make a Battlefield people want DICE so why do you refuse to do it?

[h3]Battlefield 6 – A Disappointing Decline After a Promising Start[/h3]

I genuinely enjoyed the BETA. It felt fresh, chaotic in a good way, and full of potential. But now, as the full game unfolds, Battlefield 6 is slowly sliding downhill, and the issues are becoming too big to ignore.

[h3]A Campaign That Feels Like a Tutorial[/h3]

The campaign is simply bad. There’s no weight, no excitement, and no Battlefield identity.
It plays like an extended tutorial designed to funnel you into multiplayer, not a real single-player experience worth buying the game for.

[h3]New Game Modes Bring Nothing Meaningful[/h3]

Modes like Sabotage sound interesting on paper, but in reality they add nothing valuable.
Most of these new modes take place on tiny slices of maps where 16v16 players run around in kamikaze-style chaos, spamming RPGs at objectives that give less XP than actual combat.
It’s messy, shallow, and completely disconnected from the classic Battlefield experience.

[h3]Challenges Are Not “Challenges”[/h3]

The challenge system is one of the most frustrating parts of the game.

Challenges don’t push players to try cool strategies or master their class, they simply force you into game modes you don’t want to play, like Battle Royale or Sabotage, just to check boxes and fill bars.

Why should a long-time Battlefield player who enjoys Conquest, Breakthrough, or Rush be required to grind a free Battle Royale mode to unlock gear?
Spending hours in a mode you don’t enjoy isn’t rewarding, it just creates burnout and resentment.

[h3]Spawn Issues and Small-Map Chaos[/h3]

Many new modes take place on tiny map cuts, creating constant spawn traps and unavoidable deaths. It’s a run-die-repeat loop that feels more like an arcade shooter than a large-scale tactical FPS.

[h3]Infantry Gameplay Has Lost the Battlefield Identity[/h3]

I prefer infantry gameplay, teamwork, class synergy, tactical pacing.
Battlefield 6 instead leans into constant, frantic run-and-gun action.

Playing Medic or Engineer feels unrewarding.
I end up picking Assault just to survive the chaos.


[h3]The Game Is Drifting Toward Call of Duty[/h3]

I never wanted to compare Battlefield to Call of Duty.
In fact, I always hated when people said “BF is becoming CoD.”
But after today’s session… I’m starting to see it.

This constant run-and-gun chaos, the tiny arenas, the instant deaths from five directions the moment I spawn, it all feels less and less like Battlefield and more like Call of Duty with every update.
And that’s worrying.

For the first time in over a decade of playing this franchise, I actually found myself swearing at the screen and getting angry.
That’s not healthy, and it’s not the Battlefield experience I’ve known.
Dying to a heli is normal, that’s Battlefield.
But getting deleted instantly on spawn, unable even to see the enemy, feels awful and cheap.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]

Battlefield 6 had potential, and the BETA looked promising. But the current direction feels completely disconnected from what made Battlefield special.

Forced challenges, shallow game modes, spawn frustration, and a shift toward fast arcade-style gameplay all erode the Battlefield identity.

Right now, it feels like the developers are chasing Call of Duty instead of doubling down on what their own fanbase wants.

If the game doesn’t course-correct soon, it risks losing the very community that kept the franchise alive for decades.

This review is borne out of genuine frustration. I am enjoying the core gameplay of Battlefield 6, but the current weapon and attachment unlock system is actively sucking the fun out of the game.

The challenges required to unlock basic and essential weapon attachments are excessively tedious and demanding, often requiring thousands of kills per weapon. This isn't a challenge; it's a punitive, soul-crushing grind that forces players to ignore the objective and focus on senseless metrics. It feels like the requirements were generated by an algorithm, not a team that actually plays the game.

To make matters worse, the developers have decided to target the only viable workaround: nerfing progression in Bot matches. Players were using bot matches to bypass the impossible grind in the main multiplayer modes, and instead of addressing the root problem—the ridiculous challenge requirements—the developers simply punished the players for trying to catch up.

This decision sends a clear message: "Play our game our way, even if it's not fun."

The only result of this will be player burnout. No one wants to spend dozens of hours unlocking the basic components for a single weapon. This current system is:

Anti-casual: It completely locks out players who don't have infinite time to grind.

Anti-teamplay: It encourages players to farm specific stats rather than playing the objective.

Anti-fun: The process is boring and repetitive.

DICE, you must revisit these challenges. Dial back the required numbers significantly. Stop trying to force a ludicrous grind for attachments. If the goal is player retention, this system is a spectacular failure. Right now, it feels less like a game and more like a second job, and that is not what Battlefield should be.

I've played Battlefield since 1942. The current game isn't terrible, but it just doesn't feel like a Battlefield title. It feels more like Call of Duty—and I've put in plenty of hours on COD as well. The Conquest maps mostly feel small, with only one exception. We're missing the signature large-scale, dynamic events that made past games memorable. There's no blimp exploding, no battleship crashing onto an island, no skyscraper collapsing—just a crane you can knock over.

It seems like Battlefield is trying to sit in a middle lane between traditional BF and COD gameplay, which might end up alienating fans of both. We’ll have to see how future updates shape the game, especially now that EA is in uncharted waters after being sold off.

Battlefield 6 has some fun moments

The core gunplay can be enjoyable, and the casual modes are entertaining, especially since the AI bots often play the objective surprisingly well. The visuals are also impressive, and Battlefield still delivers those signature large-scale moments that the series is known for.

That said, I ran into several issues that kept me from fully enjoying the game.

Crossplay balance is my biggest concern. Controller aim assist, particularly on consoles, feels very strong from a PC perspective. Many engagements felt like I was fighting against extremely accurate tracking, regardless of whether the opponent was using a sniper rifle or a pistol. Whether it's perfectly balanced or not, it often feels frustrating as a mouse and keyboard player.

The maps also feel quite small for the current weapon balance. SMGs are effective at surprisingly long ranges, which leads to fast-paced matches with very little downtime or tactical positioning. Movement is extremely fast, making battles feel more like constant close-quarters action than the slower, strategic Battlefield experience I was hoping for.

I've also seen increasing discussion around third-party controller adapters that allegedly enhance aim assist or vehicle controls. Even if not everyone uses them, their presence raises concerns about competitive integrity.

Performance could be better. Even on high-end PC hardware capable of well over 200 FPS, the game doesn't always feel as smooth as the frame rate suggests. There are noticeable stutters and optimization issues that take away from the experience.

The single-player campaign is short, taking roughly four hours to finish, and I didn't find it particularly memorable.

Monetization is another weak point. The store is packed with cosmetic bundles, progression can be accelerated through purchases, and it sometimes feels like spending money is encouraged more than simply playing the game. I also had a confusing experience purchasing Battlefield Pro twice, once directly and once using Battlefield Coins, and my duplicate purchase wasn't refunded.

Finally, moderation feels overly strict when it comes to chat. Players can receive lengthy chat bans for relatively minor language, while it often feels like more significant issues don't receive the same level of attention.

Overall: Battlefield 6 still has exciting moments and can be fun with friends, but as a PC player I came away disappointed by the crossplay balance, map design, optimization, monetization, and moderation. If these areas improve over time, my opinion could certainly change, but in its current state I find it difficult to recommend to players looking for a polished PC Battlefield experience.

That said, I genuinely hope the developers continue improving the game. Battlefield has always been one of my favorite franchises, and I'd love to see Battlefield 6 become the experience it has the potential to be. If DICE listens to player feedback, improves PC optimization, fine-tunes crossplay balance, and focuses on fair competition, I'll gladly revisit my review in the future. I want this game to succeed, because at its core, Battlefield still has something special.

The game has an okay base — it’s Battlefield — but the design feels weak.

The maps are boring and the balance is pretty bad. On some maps you get shot down right after taking off. And the amount of vehicles on each map feels random: too many on some maps, almost none on others.

Ground vehicles aren’t fun. The Bradley has only two useful seats, tanks feel empty, and older Battlefield games had much better vehicle gameplay.

Weapon leveling and skins are a huge grind. It takes forever and doesn’t feel worth it.

The interface looks almost copied from Call of Duty. Even if that style was popular in CoD, it doesn’t mean Battlefield should just take it. The game loses individuality because of it.

The new Redsec mode (their Battle Royale) also feels weird. Releasing a Battle Royale in 2025 feels like the trend is long gone. And the gameplay looks so much like Call of Duty that sometimes you don’t even know what game you’re in. It feels like they put a lot of effort into Redsec instead of fixing balance, making better maps, or improving vehicle systems.

Another problem is the weapons themselves. It feels like none of them really stand out. Most guns feel almost the same, just with slightly different stats. There’s no weapon that makes you think, “Yeah, I really want to play with this.”
If you think back to Battlefield 1, the guns had crazy personality — fast-firing LMGs with huge recoil, bolt-action rifles, all kinds of different playstyles. Sure, the setting was different, but the gameplay was way more interesting and varied.
In this Battlefield, the shotguns are actually fun, and running around with them is cool… but that’s basically it.

There are some good points.
The attack helicopter is fun to use.
The first-person free look is great.
And the transport helicopter guns are finally strong, so gunners can actually get kills.

But overall, nothing really stands out. It’s just a basic shooter. The new revive animation is okay, but doesn’t change much. The core is fine, but the design is weak.

Look, I just want to be honest with you all. I know it's not the same Battlefield as before, especially after Battlefield 1, 4, or Hardline. Each new game will be different, but I will say this: Battlefield is fun, and I found myself a little addicted to it when I bought it during the summer sales.

If you really love Battlefield and have lost trust in the franchise due to what happened with Battlefield 2042, I understand. However, I promise you the game is enjoyable and works well. I haven’t experienced any significant bugs so far. The maps are decent, and the classes and weapons are fun to use.

Playing with friends in squads enhances the experience because good communication makes the game even better. You don’t necessarily need to be on a call; even random players can often work together effectively. Overall, I find the game enjoyable, and I would highly recommend it to anyone who loves Battlefield but struggles to trust the series after the issues with Battlefield 2042.

One thing to note is that there aren’t any crazy skins like COD. There is a battle pass, but it’s not a big deal; you can enjoy the game without it. There is a battle royale mode, but I personally don’t like battle royale games, I tried it once and didn’t enjoy it much.

I haven’t noticed many negatives, but one thing I will mention is that there aren’t many secondary weapons available. The gadgets are good, but the challenges to unlock items for your classes can be tough. For example, to upgrade the engineer class, you need to use launchers and motion sensors launchers. I forgot the name. The one challenge I really disliked was for the support class, where you have to get 25 assist kills in smoke, which was quite frustrating.

In summary, I think the game is really fun, and I highly recommend giving it a shot. Play for about an hour or two, and if you don’t like it, you can return it. Yes, I know it’s a bit pricey, but you might want to wait for a sale or go ahead and buy it if you’re a fan of Battlefield. I hope the game continues to run well and that a player base remains as the community grows.
